cases.input:
What are the actual ideas in this passage from a draft essay I'm working on?

"Most security teams measure themselves by how many alerts they close. That number rewards the wrong behavior: a team that closes ten thousand low-value alerts looks better than one that closes forty and catches the one intrusion that matters. I've come to think the unit of security work isn't the alert, it's the decision. Every alert is a request for someone to decide something, and the cost of a security program is mostly the cost of those decisions: how long they take, how often they're wrong, and how much context the person deciding had. AI changes this because it can make the cheap decisions for us, which means the humans are left with only the expensive ones. But that creates a new problem. If the analyst only ever sees the hard cases, they lose the intuition that came from seeing thousands of easy ones. We may be automating away the apprenticeship that produces senior analysts. The fix, I think, is to deliberately route a sample of easy cases to junior people with the answer hidden, so the intuition keeps getting built even when the work itself no longer needs them."
cases.expects: A complete list of the distinct ideas in the passage (closure counts reward the wrong behavior, the decision as the unit of security work, AI taking cheap decisions, the lost apprenticeship, sampling easy cases with the answer hidden), each stated as one clear standalone bullet in plain exact words, with no repeats and nothing added that the passage does not say.

cases.input:
extract ideas from this incident review excerpt:

INCIDENT REVIEW, Northwind Logistics (fictional), payments API outage, 41 minutes.
Summary: A routine certificate rotation on the internal gateway at 02:10 UTC replaced the intermediate certificate but not the pinned fingerprint in the payments client config. Requests from the client to api.payments.example.com began failing TLS validation at 02:12. The on-call engineer was paged at 02:13 but the alert routed to a rotation that had been retired in March; the page was acknowledged by an automated escalation policy at 02:28 and reached a human at 02:34. Rollback of the certificate took 6 minutes once started. Client retries with no backoff produced a load spike of roughly 9x against the gateway at 192.0.2.40, which delayed recovery by about 11 minutes after the certificate was restored.
Contributing factors discussed: (1) certificate rotation has no staging step; (2) fingerprint pinning is undocumented outside the client repo; (3) the paging policy was never audited after the team reorg; (4) retry logic was copied from a batch job where load did not matter.
Action items: add a staging gate to rotation, document pinning, audit all paging policies quarterly, add jittered exponential backoff to the payments client.
Note from the reviewer: "We keep treating outages as one failure when they are usually four small ones lining up."
cases.expects: The distinct ideas and lessons from the review as separate standalone bullets, covering the technical causes, the paging and retry failures, the action items and the reviewer's closing observation, each in plain exact words with nothing duplicated and no invented causes or numbers.
